Students will analyze how his informal, sarcastic word choices shape the tone of the opening and a reader’s first impression of him. Students will consider how these pages might set Percy up as a hero or a “problem” figure in a modern myth."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will use morphology (mort-, -ology, trans-) to work out the meaning of immortal and related myth words. Students will use context to confirm the meanings of the other unit words during reading. Students will expand sentences with adverbials (when, how, why) to add detail to their inferences."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will use word parts (roots and affixes) to figure out and verify word meanings, then add this lesson’s words to their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers."}],"essentialQuestions":["How do Percy’s comments in the opening pages show his world values (and fears) about “normal” kids, and how might these opening pages be setting him up to become a hero or “problem” figure in a modern myth?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"In Lesson 3, students heard Rick Riordan explain what myths do for people and why he adapts them. Today they meet Percy’s voice for the first time and look for early clues about the modern myth Riordan is building.","enduringUnderstanding":"Narrators reveal what they value and fear through their word choices. Those choices shape tone and give readers a first impression, and early details begin to point toward a story’s theme.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 5 students will write an explanatory paragraph about Chapter 1 (pp. 9–15) with a clear topic sentence, relevant evidence and a concluding statement. Today students collect the first pieces of evidence about “normal” versus different, and they practice stating a tentative theme apart from their opinions."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"envy","definition":"to feel unhappy because you want something another person has","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"recognize","definition":"to know someone or something because you have seen or felt it before; here, to see yourself in something","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"frayed","definition":"worn and coming apart at the edges, like old rope or cloth","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"expelled","definition":"officially forced to leave a school as a punishment","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"probation","definition":"a trial period in which someone’s behavior is watched, with punishment if they break the rules","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"threatened","definition":"said that something bad would happen, especially a punishment","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"spawn","definition":"the offspring of a creature; in myth and informal speech, a child of a monster or a god, sometimes used as an insult","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"detention","definition":"a punishment in which a student must stay after school","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"immortal","definition":"living forever; not able to die","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"dyslexia","definition":"a learning difference that makes reading, spelling and writing harder","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mortal","definition":"a being that will die someday","tier":"support"},{"word":"mythology","definition":"a collection of traditional stories about gods, heroes and monsters; also the study of those stories","tier":"support"},{"word":"transform","definition":"to change form or appearance completely","tier":"support"},{"word":"transport","definition":"to carry something or someone from one place to another","tier":"support"},{"word":"sarcastic","definition":"saying the opposite of what you mean to mock or show annoyance","tier":"support"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the attitude a writer or narrator shows toward a subject through word choice","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 1, pp. 1–8 (Teacher Read Aloud)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students connect Riordan’s view of what myths do for people (Lesson 3) to the idea of a “normal” kid and begin thinking about what makes someone a hero or a “problem.”","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"What Makes Someone “Normal”?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner. Answer the question on the board. Take turns, and use the sentence starter: “Being ‘normal’ at school means ___.”"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Yesterday we heard Rick Riordan explain what he thinks myths do for people. Today we meet Percy Jackson. First, think about your own school: what does it mean to be a “normal” kid, and what might a kid fear about being seen as not normal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Being normal means you fit in, like you wear the same stuff and you’re not the one getting in trouble. A kid might be scared of being the one everyone laughs at or being left out at lunch."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold on to that idea. Today we listen to Percy’s own voice in the opening pages. We will look for what he values, what he fears, and whether this opening is setting him up to be a hero or a problem in a modern myth."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 3 minutes of talk. Take two or three shares, then move on. You are only activating ideas about “normal.” The evidence work comes later."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students use morphology tied to myth language to figure out immortal. They preview this lesson’s other unit words, which they will confirm in context during the read aloud, and record them in their Unit Vocabulary organizers.","activities":[{"id":"lab-morphology-word-building","title":"Word Building: mort-, -ology, trans-","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Word-Building Routine","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Ten words is a lot for depth work. Go deep on immortal through morphology. The other nine get quick, in-context treatment in the next activity and during reading. The mort-, -ology and trans- words are myth language students will see throughout the unit."},{"type":"directions","text":"Watch the word parts on the board. Say each word with me. Use the parts to guess what each word means, then check your guess with a partner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Many myth words are built from Latin and Greek parts. The root mort- comes from Latin and means “death.” Add the prefix im-, which means “not,” and you have immortal, a word on page 6 of today’s reading."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If mort- means death, and im- means not, what does immortal mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Immortal means not able to die, so it means living forever. Gods in myths are immortal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What would mortal mean, then? Who in a Greek myth would be mortal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortal means able to die, so regular humans. In a Greek myth the humans are mortal and the gods are immortal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Now the suffix -ology. It comes from Greek and means “the study of.” Myth plus -ology gives mythology, the study or collection of myths. Last, the prefix trans- means “across” or “change.” Transport means to carry across. Transform means to change form."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"A myth character “transforms” into a bird. Using trans-, what happened?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He changed across into a different form. Trans- means change, so he became a bird."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Always verify your guess. Check that the meaning fits the sentence, or check a dictionary. Our word-part guess for immortal gets a quick check when we hear it read aloud."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners connect word parts to meaning and use cognates from their home languages. Language focus: roots, prefixes and suffixes in myth vocabulary.","sayAsk":"Say the words aloud with students (mort-, immortal, mortal). Point out cognates: Spanish mortal and inmortal, mitología, transformar, transportar. Ask: Which word part helped you? Frames: The root mort- means ___. Immortal means ___ because im- means ___ and mort- means ___. Transform means ___ because trans- means ___.","watchFor":"If students memorize the word without using the parts, then ask: Which part tells you “not”? Which tells you “death”? If students guess from the sound of the word only, then ask them to find the prefix and root first. Success: the student explains meaning using at least two word parts."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: using word parts to infer meaning","tryThis":"Give a word-part card (mort- = death, im- = not) and have students physically combine the cards, then say the meaning in their own words. Use the frame “___ means ___ because ___ + ___.”"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find or invent another word with mort- (mortality, mortician, mortify) or trans- (translate, transition) and explain how the word part helps reveal the meaning."}]}]},{"id":"lab-vocab-preview-organizer","title":"Preview Unit Words and Start Organizers","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d","L.6.6"],"routine":"Vocabulary Graphic Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Add these words: envy, recognize, frayed, expelled, probation, threatened, spawn, detention, immortal, dyslexia. Write the word and a first guess or a home-language connection now. You will confirm each meaning with the page when we read."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Don’t worry, we won’t memorize ten definitions. I’ll group them so they are easier to hold, and we will confirm each one in the sentence as we read. Say each word after me."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Present the words in three quick clusters (about 30 seconds each). Say the word, give the kid-friendly meaning from the vocabulary list, and have students repeat. Feelings and stance: envy (p. 1), recognize (p. 1), threatened (p. 3). School trouble: expelled (p. 2), probation (p. 3), detention (p. 4). Describing and labeling: frayed (p. 2), spawn (p. 4), dyslexia (p. 7). Immortal (p. 6) was done through morphology. Students record only a first guess and a page number."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at expelled, probation and detention. What do these three words have in common, and what does that make you predict about Percy’s school life?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They are all school punishments. I predict Percy gets in trouble a lot at school."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Frayed and recognize are multiple-meaning words. Tell students you will check how each one is used in the sentence, since frayed can describe rope or nerves, and recognize can mean know someone or see yourself in something."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students listen to a fluent read aloud of pp. 1–8, follow the teacher’s think-alouds, and confirm vocabulary in context. Part B: Students cite evidence to make inferences and predictions about Percy’s values and fears and about hero versus “problem” figure. Part C: Students analyze informal, sarcastic word choices and how they shape tone and first impressions.","activities":[{"id":"lia-read-aloud-think-aloud","title":"Part A: Teacher Read Aloud with Think-Alouds (pp. 1–8)","minutes":11,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.6","L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d"],"routine":"Teacher Read Aloud / Think-Aloud","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Follow along in your book as I read. Put a star by any line that shows what Percy values or fears, and underline a word that shows his attitude. Jot a quick note when I stop to think aloud."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Model engaging fluency. Slow down on the opening warning, use a dry, flat voice for sarcastic lines, speed up for exasperated lists, and pause before key lines. Stop only four times so the read aloud flows. Page numbers vary by edition, so rely on the vocabulary page markers and the opening lines."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 1, opening lines. (Read: “Look, I didn’t want to be a half-blood.”) Think-aloud: Right away the narrator says “Look,” like he is talking to me. He sounds annoyed and honest. He also says he didn’t want this, so I’m already wondering who he is and why he’s so reluctant."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 2, the warning to readers. (Read his advice to close the book and lead a normal life.) Think-aloud: He tells readers to stop reading and try to “lead a normal life.” That tells me he thinks normal is safe, and being a half-blood is dangerous. I’m going to star this as a value and a fear. Now I’m checking the word envy: he says he envies people who can believe none of it happened. I’ll check my guess: envy means wanting what someone else has, so he wishes he could be one of the normal kids."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 3, school trouble on pp. 2–4. (Read the lines using expelled, probation, threatened and detention.) Think-aloud: Percy keeps getting into trouble. When I read the sentence with expelled, I confirm it means he was kicked out of school. Probation means someone is watching to see if he behaves, and threatened means he was warned of a punishment. The word spawn is a surprise in a school setting, because spawn is something I connect with monsters. I’ll keep my eye on that, since a myth can hide in a school story."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Stop 4, pp. 6–7. (Read the passages with immortal and dyslexia.) Think-aloud: Immortal fits my word-part guess, because it is used about beings who can’t die, so the myth world is leaking in. Dyslexia is how he explains why reading is hard for him, so he may see himself as not normal in school. I wonder if what makes him different will turn out to matter."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Turn to a partner. Which word from our list did we confirm in the sentence, and how did the sentence help?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"We confirmed expelled. The sentence says he was kicked out of school, so the meaning “forced to leave school” fits. For frayed, the sentence describes something worn out and falling apart, not just rope."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in reading closely by listening, following along and confirming word meanings in context. Language focus: following a read aloud, noticing attitude words.","sayAsk":"Before reading, give students a one-sentence preview: “Percy talks directly to the reader and warns them.” Ask: Which word helped you understand how Percy feels? Frames: Percy sounds ___ because he says ___. The word ___ means ___ in this sentence. I confirmed it because the sentence says ___.","watchFor":"If students cannot follow the pace, then re-read the opening paragraph and have them track with a finger or a bookmark. If students star only exciting events and not feelings, then ask: What does this line show Percy wants or is afraid of? Success: the student marks at least one value or fear and can say why."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: following the read aloud and tracking details","tryThis":"Give a half-sheet with the four stops and one line for each. Students write one word per stop, such as annoyed, normal, trouble, different. Pause after each stop for a quick partner retell."},{"type":"situation-placeholder","tryThis":""}]}]},{"id":"lia-cite-evidence-infer-predict","title":"Part B: Evidence, Inferences and Predictions About Percy","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Annotation and Evidence Chart","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Make a three-column chart: What Percy says (quote or paraphrase with page number), What I infer about his values or fears, What I predict about his story. Fill in at least two rows with your partner. Use “Percy says… so I infer… which makes me predict…”"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"An inference combines something the text says with what you already know. A good inference points to specific words. A prediction says what might happen next because of that evidence. A theme or central idea is a larger message the story starts to build, and today we only collect early clues, so we call it a tentative theme."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy’s advice to “lead a normal life” and his statement that he envies readers who believe it’s fiction show about what he values and fears?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy says he envies people who think none of it happened and tells readers to lead a normal life. I infer he values being normal and safe, and he fears being different, because being a half-blood is dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Based on that evidence, how might these pages set Percy up as a hero or a “problem” in a modern myth?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both could be true. He keeps getting expelled and put on probation, so the adults see him as a problem kid. But he warns readers like he has survived something dangerous, and heroes in myths often start out as outsiders. I predict the things that make him seem like a problem will turn out to be part of his power."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using only the text, how would you state a tentative theme or central idea in one sentence, and how is that different from your opinion?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A tentative theme is: Feeling different or “not normal” can be scary, but it may also be the beginning of something important. That is not my opinion about whether I like Percy. It is what the details so far suggest."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Early in Chapter 1, what does Percy tell readers who think they might be half-bloods?","choices":[{"text":"He tells them to stop reading and try to live a normal life because being a half-blood is dangerous.","correct":true,"rationale":"Percy warns readers to close the book and lead a normal life, and he says being a half-blood is dangerous."},{"text":"He tells them to keep reading because being a half-blood is exciting and safe.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses his message. He warns readers away and says it is dangerous, not safe."},{"type":"x","text":"","correct":false,"rationale":""},{"text":"He tells them the story is made up, so they have nothing to worry about.","correct":false,"rationale":"He does tell readers who think it’s fiction to read on, but he warns the ones who recognize themselves. He does not say the story is made up."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in explaining inferences and predictions and adding detail to sentences. Language focus: inference verbs (shows, suggests) and adverbials of time, manner and cause.","sayAsk":"Model a sentence and then expand it. Base: Percy warns readers. Expanded: Because being a half-blood is dangerous, Percy warns readers at the very start of the book. Ask: Which words tell why, when or how? Frames: Percy says ___, which shows ___. At the beginning, ___ suggests ___. Because ___, I predict ___.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot instead of inferring, then ask: What does that detail show about what Percy wants or fears? If students write short sentences with no detail, then ask them to add when, how or why. Success: the student connects a quote to an inference with a verb like shows or suggests and adds at least one adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: moving from quote to inference","tryThis":"Provide a pre-filled quote for the row and ask two questions: What does Percy want? What is he afraid of? Students answer orally, then write one sentence with the frame “Percy says ___, so I infer ___.”"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to write a tentative theme sentence and name a detail on p. 4 or p. 7 that could challenge or complicate it. Ask what they need to read next to check it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-tone-word-choice","title":"Part C: Informal, Sarcastic Word Choice and Tone","minutes":9,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.6","L.6.4","L.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Close Read and Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the first paragraph or two on p. 1 and one other passage where Percy sounds sarcastic or casual. Copy two phrases that sound informal or sarcastic. For each one, write what it makes you feel about Percy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Tone is the attitude the narrator shows toward a subject, and it comes from word choice. Informal words sound like everyday talk, like “Look,” and sarcasm says the opposite of what you mean to show frustration or humor. Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which informal or sarcastic words or phrases in the opening pages stood out to you, and what tone do they create?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"“Look, I didn’t want to be a half-blood” sounds like someone talking to a friend, annoyed and defensive. The tone is blunt and a little grumpy, which makes Percy sound real and honest."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What first impression of Percy does this tone create, and how does it connect to his fear of not being normal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It makes me think Percy is funny, honest and kind of a rebel, but also tired of being the problem kid. The sarcasm could be his way of covering up that he is scared of being different."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at a word like spawn or frayed. What feeling or connotation does it carry, and how is it different from a plain synonym?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Spawn sounds nastier and more monstrous than child, so it makes the insult feel harsh. Frayed sounds worn and stressed, so it shows things are not holding together, more than just old."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.6"],"stem":"How do Percy’s informal word choices, such as opening with “Look,” shape the tone of the opening pages?","choices":[{"text":"They make Percy sound like he is talking directly to the reader in a blunt, annoyed, honest voice.","correct":true,"rationale":"“Look” and similar everyday phrasing create a casual, blunt tone, and the narrator seems to speak straight to the reader."},{"text":"They make the opening sound formal and serious, like a history textbook.","correct":false,"rationale":"The language is casual, not formal. Students may confuse a serious warning with a formal tone."},{"text":"They show that Percy is proud and excited to be a half-blood.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy says he did not want to be a half-blood, so his tone is reluctant, not proud."},{"text":"They show that the narrator does not care what happens to the readers.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy’s warning shows he does care. His blunt style hides concern for the reader."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners evaluate how language choices create tone and add details to sentences. Language focus: tone words, connotation, adverbs of manner.","sayAsk":"Offer a tone word bank (blunt, sarcastic, annoyed, honest, nervous, funny). Model: Percy speaks bluntly to the reader. Then expand: Percy speaks bluntly and honestly to the reader because he wants to protect them. Frames: The phrase ___ creates a ___ tone. This word choice makes Percy sound ___ because ___. Percy speaks ___ (how) because ___ (why).","watchFor":"If students say only “he sounds mad,” then ask them to quote the words that sound mad and name a more precise tone word. If students confuse sarcasm with meanness, then ask: Does he say the opposite of what he means to be funny or to show frustration? Success: the student names a tone, quotes a phrase and explains the effect on a reader’s first impression."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: naming tone from word choice","tryThis":"Give a short tone word bank and have students match one quoted phrase to one tone word. Then have them complete “The word ___ makes Percy sound ___.”"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite one of Percy’s lines in a formal voice and compare the two versions. Ask how the change would alter the reader’s first impression and the story’s mood."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students summarize what Percy’s opening reveals and tie today’s evidence to the Performance Task skill of identifying emerging themes.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Complete the Claim: Percy’s Opening","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task you will explain themes, the big ideas stories share, using evidence. Today you collected the first clues about what this modern myth might say about being normal and being different."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the paragraph: In the opening pages of The Lightning Thief, Percy shows that he values ___ and fears ___. One detail that shows this is ___ (page ___). This makes me predict that Percy will become a ___ because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the opening pages of The Lightning Thief, Percy shows that he values being normal and safe and fears being different and in danger. One detail that shows this is that he tells readers to close the book and lead a normal life. This makes me predict that Percy will become a hero because the things that make him seem like a problem, like getting expelled, may actually be signs that he is special."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect these as an exit check. Look for a specific detail, a stated value or fear, and a prediction connected to evidence rather than a personal opinion."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Students continue reading and annotating to prepare for Lesson 5 and to begin comparing a modern myth with an older story.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-annotate","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Optional. 1) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1 (pp. 9–15). Star any detail that shows what Percy values or fears, and underline words that show his tone. 2) Read and annotate the excerpt from “The Hare and the Lion.” Note what each character wants and any lesson the story seems to teach."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Lesson 5 is a writing lesson using Chapter 1 (pp. 9–15), so students’ annotations will become evidence for their explanatory paragraph."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students listened to a teacher read aloud of The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1 (pp. 1–8), with think-alouds. They cited evidence to infer Percy’s values and fears about being “normal,” predicted whether he is headed to be a hero or a “problem,” and analyzed how his informal, sarcastic word choices create tone. Vocabulary was taught through morphology (mort-, -ology, trans-) and confirmed in context.","keyActivities":["Turn and Talk on what “normal” means at school","Word-building routine with mort-, -ology and trans-, focused on immortal","Vocabulary preview in clusters and organizer setup for ten unit words","Teacher read aloud of pp. 1–8 with four think-alouds","Three-column evidence chart: what Percy says, inference, prediction","Close read of informal and sarcastic word choice and tone","Look Back paragraph frame on values, fears and a hero or “problem” prediction"],"vocabularyTaught":["envy","recognize","frayed","expelled","probation","threatened","spawn","detention","immortal","dyslexia","mortal","mythology","transform","transport","sarcastic","tone"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","RL.6.4","RL.6.5","RL.6.6","RL.6.10","L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d","L.6.5","L.6.6"]}}
